title: Dolma yaprak
subtitle: Stuffed vine leaves with rice, pine nuts, and currants
excerpt: Dolma yaprak are rolled vine leaves stuffed with a lemony rice mixture of pine nuts, currants, and fresh herbs. The vegetarian version is served cold or at room temperature as a starter or meze, with a good squeeze of lemon. They take patience to roll but keep well for several days.
sourceNotes: Claudia Roden, A Book of Middle Eastern Food (1968). Stuffed vine leaves documented across Greece, Turkey, and the Arab world, with the vegetarian version described as the Turkish yalanci dolma (false dolma, served cold). Aylin Oney Tan, A Taste of Sun and Fire (2014). Regional variations across Turkey and the Levant.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to three days ahead and refrigerate. The flavour improves over time. Serve at room temperature, not cold from the fridge.

content.text: Dolma yaprak are vine leaves rolled tightly around a rice filling of pine nuts, currants, onion, and fresh herbs. The stuffed rolls are packed into a pot and simmered in olive oil and lemon until the rice is cooked and the leaves are very tender. Served at room temperature, they are one of the most characteristic meze dishes of the eastern Mediterranean.

items.prepNote: jarred in brine, drained and rinsed

content.text: Combine {{long-grain-rice}}, {{onion}}, {{pine-nuts}}, {{currants}}, {{parsley-flat}}, {{mint}}, {{dill}}, {{cinnamon-ground}}, {{allspice}}, {{sea-salt-fine}}, and 2 tablespoons of the {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} in a bowl. Mix well. The rice is used raw.

Lay a {{vine-leaves}} leaf flat on a board, rough side up. Place a heaped teaspoon of filling near the stem end. Fold the sides of the leaf in over the filling, then roll up from the stem end into a tight cylinder. Do not roll too tightly as the rice expands. Repeat with all the remaining leaves and filling.
Line the base of a wide, heavy saucepan with a few spare vine leaves (to prevent sticking). Pack the rolls in tight layers, seam side down.

Mix the remaining {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}}, lemon juice from {{lemon}}, {{caster-sugar}}, and 300 ml of water together. Pour over the rolls. The liquid should just cover them; add more water if needed.

Place a small heatproof plate directly on top of the rolls to keep them submerged. Bring to the boil, then reduce to the lowest possible simmer. Cover and cook for 45 to 50 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and the liquid is mostly absorbed.
Leave to cool in the pan. Transfer to a serving plate with any remaining cooking juices spooned over. Serve at room temperature with extra lemon wedges.

items.symptom: The rolls are unravelling in the pot
items.cause: Not rolled tightly enough or packed loosely in the pot
items.fix: Pack the rolls snugly in layers: tight packing holds them together during cooking. A plate on top also helps.

items.symptom: The rice is still undercooked after fifty minutes
items.cause: Not enough liquid or heat too low
items.fix: Add another 100 ml of boiling water, cover, and cook for another fifteen minutes. The liquid must be simmering throughout.

items.cause: Leaves not rinsed properly, retaining excess brine
items.fix: Rinse jarred leaves thoroughly in cold water and blanch in boiling water for two minutes before rolling to soften them.

items.symptom: The filling tastes bland when the rolls are cool
items.cause: Filling was not seasoned assertively enough
items.fix: Season the filling before rolling. The flavour should taste slightly over-seasoned raw, as the rice absorbs salt during cooking.

content.text: Stuffed vine leaves appear across a wide arc of cuisines from Greece to Iran, but the vegetarian cold version with rice, pine nuts, and currants is particularly associated with Turkish and Greek cooking. The Turkish name yalanci dolma (false dolma) distinguishes these from the meat-stuffed warm version. The sweet-sour-savoury balance of currants, lemon, and herbs is the defining character. In Turkey, dolma yaprak is a standard meze at meyhane (taverns) and at home gatherings. The rolling technique is passed down directly in families, and the ability to roll quickly and neatly is a kitchen skill worth developing.
